blocks.text: Nor did this escape Fuller. So, in order not to be forced to recognize ostriches here, he devises something else, namely that in the Greek version στρουθούς [strouthous] are owls, or rather screech owls [striges]. He tries to prove this with two arguments, but both are entirely invalid. The first is as follows. In Suidas στρουθίζων [strouthizōn] is explained as τρίζων [trizōn], screeching, which is proper to screech owls; therefore στρουθός [strouthos] too, from which στρουθίζειν [strouthizein] comes, is a strix [screech owl]. And that this is proper to screech owls he proves from the sixth book of the Fasti, where Ovid says:
Their name is striges; but the reason for this name is that they are wont to screech horribly at night.
As in the little poem On the Nightingale, whoever its author may be:
The screech owl sounding by night, and the bat, screech.
But this is adduced in vain, since τρίζειν [trizein] belongs to sparrows as well. Thus in Iliad β΄ [2], line 314, the dragon [devoured] eight little sparrows with their mother:

it devoured them piteously as they twittered. Since, then, τρίζειν [trizein] belongs as much to sparrows as to screech owls, when Suidas explains στρουθίζων [strouthizōn] as τρίζων [trizōn], he could have had in view the chirping of sparrows just as well as the screeching of owls. And indeed it is taken from Esa. X, 14., where for the Hebrew מצפצף, that is, chattering like little birds or twittering, the Greek version has στρουθίζων [strouthizōn], which Theodoret explains as τρίσαι [trisai], to screech, and γρύζειν στρουθοῖς [II, 818] παραπλησίως [gryzein strouthois paraplēsiōs], to chirp like sparrows. So there was no reason for Fuller to imagine here the screeching and hooting of owls. But he aims another weapon, which will seem stronger. Strix, he says, is rendered in the Glossary not only as ὀλολυγών [ololygōn], that is, owl, but also as στρουθός [strouthos]. For there it reads thus: Strix, Ὀλολυγών, στρουθός [Ololygōn, strouthos]. Therefore these three, strix, ὀλολυγών [ololygōn] and στρουθός [strouthos], are synonyms. I reply that this passage of the Glossary is plainly corrupt. For it has never been heard that the word στρουθός [strouthos] means either a strix or an owl. So that στρουθός [strouthos] has been moved from its place and must be put back lower down, after the words Struthio, Στρουθοκάμηλος [Strouthokamēlos]. Such transposition of words is frequent in the Glosses. Thus in the same: Facundus, Εὔγλωττος, γόνιμος [Euglōttos, gonimos]; the last of these belongs to Foecundus or Foecunda, which follow below. Likewise, Fastus, Ἐπισκύνιον, ἡμερολόγιον [Episkynion, hēmerologion]; the latter means fasti [calendar], not fastus [pride]. It therefore belonged to the word Fasti, which has been omitted. In the same place, Rigor, Κρύος, ἀπόσκληρον [Kryos, aposklēron]; of these, ἀπόσκληρον [aposklēron] must be referred to rigidum, which follows. And in Hesychius: Ἀλύω· ἀδημονῶ, ἀθυμῶ· Φοίνικες [Alyō; adēmonō, athymō; Phoinikes]. Absurd: for the verb ἀλύω [alyō] cannot be a Phoenician word. So the word Φοίνικες [Phoinikes] has been moved from its place, and belongs to what follows, Ἄλφα· βοὸς κεφαλή [Alpha; boos kephalē]. And this itself is not free from error. [col. 223] For one must write βοῦς, κεφαλή [bous, kephalē], as we have noted elsewhere. The passage of the Glossary under discussion can also be restored otherwise: namely if for στρουθός [strouthos] one reads στρίγλος [striglos], which was the name of the strix among the Greeks, as these words of Hesychius prove, though very corrupt: Στρίγλος· τὰ ἐντὸς τοῦ κέρατος, νυκτίφοιτον. Καλεῖται δὲ καὶ νυκτοβόα, οἱ δὲ νυκτικόρακα [Striglos; ta entos tou keratos, nyktiphoiton. Kaleitai de kai nyktoboa, hoi de nyktikoraka]. I think these should be written thus: Στρίγλος· τὸ ἐν τοῖς τερατείοις νυκτίφοιτον [Striglos; to en tois terateiois nyktiphoiton] etc. Among uncanny things, that which walks by night; it is also called nycti-boa (as it were, crying by night) and by some nycti-corax.
